summary: Describes Hybrid Public Key Encryption, a way to encrypt data of any size to a recipient's public key. It combines a key encapsulation mechanism, a key derivation function, and an authenticated encryption algorithm, and includes authenticated variants. It is informational.

eli5.summary: You lock a box with a key only the receiver can open, but a quick lock is used for the heavy contents inside.

questions: how does hybrid public key encryption work
how does hpke differ from ecies
subtitle: A standard recipe for encrypting data of any size to someone's public key, built from a KEM, a KDF and an AEAD.

tldr.problem: Existing hybrid encryption schemes, mostly variants of ECIES, are competing and non-interoperable, and many rely on outdated primitives, lack proofs of IND-CCA2 security, or fail to provide test vectors.
tldr.mechanism: HPKE encapsulates a fresh symmetric key to the recipient's public key with a key encapsulation mechanism, runs it through a key schedule built on a key derivation function, and then encrypts messages with an AEAD. Four modes optionally add a pre-shared key, a sender key pair, or both.
tldr.outcome: It gives a clearly specified, interoperable scheme that is IND-CCA2-secure under classical assumptions. It is a low-level building block: it leaves message encoding, ordering, replay and downgrade protection to the application.

today: RFC 9180 is an Informational document and has not been obsoleted or updated. It remains the specification of HPKE for the algorithms listed in its registries.

sections.title: What HPKE Is For
sections.content:
Hybrid schemes combine the key management advantages of asymmetric cryptography with the performance of symmetric cryptography. The traditional approach is to encrypt the symmetric key with the public key. Hybrid Public Key Encryption (HPKE) instead generates the symmetric key together with its encapsulation under the public key. An encrypted message conveys the encapsulated key plus one or more arbitrary-sized ciphertexts encrypted with that key. The RFC names Messaging Layer Security and TLS Encrypted ClientHello as applications.

The RFC says the existing standards, mostly variants of the Elliptic Curve Integrated Encryption Scheme (ECIES), have problems: outdated primitives, no proofs of IND-CCA2 security, or no test vectors. HPKE provides a subset of their functions, specified clearly enough to be implemented interoperably. The document represents the consensus of the Crypto Forum Research Group (CFRG).
sections.eli5: Instead of sending a big heavy parcel in a special lock that is slow to use, you send a small key in the special lock, and then lock the big parcel with a fast ordinary lock.

sections.title: The Three Building Blocks
sections.content:
HPKE relies on three primitives. A key encapsulation mechanism (KEM) offers GenerateKeyPair(), DeriveKeyPair(), Encap(pkR) and Decap(enc, skR), plus optional AuthEncap() and AuthDecap(). Encap produces a fresh shared secret and an encapsulation enc that only the holder of the recipient private key can open. A key derivation function (KDF) provides Extract() and Expand(). An AEAD provides Seal() and Open().

A ciphersuite is a triple (KEM, KDF, AEAD). Algorithm identifiers are two bytes long. The document defines DHKEM, a KEM built from a Diffie-Hellman group and a KDF, and its Auth variants are vulnerable to key-compromise impersonation. Calls into the KDF are domain-separated by LabeledExtract and LabeledExpand, which mix in the string HPKE-v1 and a suite_id.
sections.eli5: There are three tools: one that seals a secret in a box only the receiver can open, one that mixes ingredients into a good key, and one that scrambles the actual message and notices if anyone touched it.

sections.title: Modes, Key Schedule and Encryption
sections.content:
All variants take the recipient public key and produce an encapsulated key enc and ciphertexts. Every variant follows two steps: set up an encryption context shared by sender and recipient, then use it to encrypt or decrypt. There are four modes, identified by a one-byte value: mode_base (0x00), mode_psk (0x01), mode_auth (0x02) and mode_auth_psk (0x03). The PSK modes let the recipient check that the sender held a pre-shared key, which MUST have at least 32 bytes of entropy. The Auth modes check that the sender held a KEM private key, but they authenticate only the key pair, not any other identity.

A common key schedule turns the mode, shared secret, application info, and optional psk and psk_id into a key, a base_nonce and an exporter_secret. A context can then encrypt many messages. The nonce for each message is base_nonce XORed with a sequence number that starts at 0 and increments per operation; on overflow the implementation MUST fail with an error. Encryption is unidirectional from sender to recipient.

The secret export interface derives extra secrets from the context, similar to the TLS 1.3 exporter. Single-shot APIs such as Seal<MODE> and Open<MODE> wrap setup and one encryption for the common case of a single message.
sections.eli5: There are four ways to lock the box: just the receiver's public lock, plus a shared password, plus proof of who you are, or both. After the box is set up, you can put many letters through it in order, and each gets its own numbered tag.

sections.title: Algorithm Identifiers
sections.content:
Section 7 lists the initial algorithms. The KEMs are DHKEM over P-256, P-384, P-521, X25519 and X448, each paired with an HKDF hash. The KDFs are HKDF-SHA256, HKDF-SHA384 and HKDF-SHA512. The AEADs are AES-128-GCM, AES-256-GCM and ChaCha20Poly1305, plus an Export-only identifier 0xFFFF for applications that use only the export interface.

The RFC states that the length limits on psk, psk_id, info and exporter_context are very large, and recommends a limit of 64 bytes for interoperability with implementations that allocate memory statically. Future KEMs, KDFs and AEADs may be added if they meet the security requirements of the document.
sections.eli5: It is like a menu: you pick one kind of lock, one kind of mixer and one kind of scrambler, and each choice has a short number so both sides can agree on it.

sections.title: Security Properties and Non-Goals
sections.content:
The goals are message secrecy against chosen ciphertext attacks, export key secrecy, and sender authentication in the PSK, Auth and AuthPSK modes. The RFC cites analyses showing IND-CCA2 security under classical assumptions about the primitives.

HPKE is deliberately low-level. It does not provide forward secrecy with respect to recipient compromise: someone who steals the long-term recipient key can decrypt past ciphertexts. It is forward secret with respect to sender compromise. The DHKEM Auth modes are vulnerable to key-compromise impersonation, and the RFC suggests a digital signature over the (enc, ct) tuple for applications that need resistance. Ciphertexts MUST be opened in the order they were sealed, and a lost message means the application MUST discard the context.

HPKE gives no downgrade prevention, no replay protection beyond ordering within a context, and does not hide plaintext length. Bad ephemeral randomness can degrade confidentiality significantly, up to losing it completely in Base mode.

A pre-shared key can help preserve security if a non-quantum-resistant KEM is broken by a quantum computer, as long as the key has not been compromised.
sections.eli5: The special box is strong, but it does not stop someone who steals the receiver's key from opening old boxes, and it cannot tell whether a letter went missing. Those jobs are left to the people using it.

sections.title: Message Encoding and IANA Registries
sections.content:
HPKE defines no wire format. Applications must specify an unambiguous encoding that includes at least the encapsulated value enc, the ciphertext values and their order, and any info values that are not implicit, such as which recipient public key was used when the recipient has more than one.

IANA created three registries under Hybrid Public Key Encryption, for KEM, KDF and AEAD identifiers. All are two-byte values with a Specification Required policy, and their initial contents are the tables in the RFC.
sections.eli5: The recipe says how to lock the box but not how to write the address label. Each program has to decide that itself, and there is an official list of numbers for the lock types.

items.label: mode_base
items.desc: Encrypt to a public key; no sender authentication.

items.label: mode_psk
items.desc: Adds a pre-shared key so the recipient can authenticate it.

items.label: mode_auth
items.desc: Recipient authenticates that the sender held a KEM private key.

items.label: mode_auth_psk
items.desc: Combines the PSK and asymmetric-key authentication.
